edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id on every page: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PVTU9" (same template fix applies to all six pages).

edits.quote: Play with a partner, using real counters. Take turns taking counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins.
edits.fix: P1, P2, P3 and P6 all hinge on "can always win", which the K-1 page never defines (the other bands do). Add one sentence to the shared rules: "You can always win if you win no matter what your partner does."

edits.quote: Circle the number under each pile where your partner can always win if you go first.
edits.fix: Put the condition first so it is not lost when read aloud and the switch from P1 (stars for your wins) to circles for your partner's wins is clear: "You go first. Circle the number under each pile where your partner can always win."

edits.quote: Circle 1st or 2nd to show whether you would rather go first or second.
edits.fix: Cut the repetition: "Circle whether you would rather go 1st or 2nd." (matches P7).

k-1.summary: A solid K-1 sequence: six small {1,2} piles to classify, choosing the winning move, finding traps up to 15, a strategy test against an adult, then two new rules ({1,2,3} and the odd/even {1,3}) and two-row mirror games; every diagram and expected answer checks out. Edits are small: the footer id, defining "always win" on this page, and two wording trims. A quick first grader might run short a little before forty minutes, but there is no real volume gap.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id on every page: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PVTU9".

edits.quote: Who can always win? (printed after each of (a)-(d))
edits.fix: The stem already asks the question; delete the four repeated "Who can always win?" labels and leave one answer line (1st or 2nd) per rule.

grades-2-3.summary: The strongest band: {1,2} piles to 20 and to 45, then the {1,3,4} game classified to 20 (losers 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), claim-testing that exposes the greedy take-4 error, extension to 30/50/100 via the period-7 pattern, two-row starts such as (1,4) and (3,6) that are second-player wins without being mirror images, and a comparison of four rules at 35. All expected answers are correct and the prose is lean. Only the footer and one repeated label need changing.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id on every page: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PVTU9".

edits.quote: Explain why the pattern you found keeps going the same way forever, so that you can be sure of your answers.
edits.fix: Delete "so that you can be sure of your answers"; the request to explain why the pattern continues forever already does the work.

edits.quote: (a) Take 1, 2, or 4 ... (b) Take 1, 2, or 5 ... (c) Take 1, 2, or 6 ... (d) Take 1, 2, or 7 counters on each turn.
edits.fix: Only (c) changes the multiples-of-3 pattern (to losers 3, 7, 10, 14, 17, 21, 24); 4, 5 and 7 all leave it unchanged. With one changing case children cannot tell that the extra number being a multiple of 3 is what matters. Replace (d) with "Take 1, 2, or 9" so two contrasting cases change.

edits.quote: (d) Only the pile of 3, and no other pile.
edits.fix: The answer depends on whether a rule may be an endless list: "take any number except 3" makes 3 the only losing pile, while any finite list fails (a pile bigger than 3 plus the largest move can reach neither 0 nor 3). Say in the stem that a rule is a finite list of numbers, or put both readings in the adult notes.

edits.quote: Gray pre-shaded square at (0,0) in both grids, not mentioned in the text
edits.fix: Either remove the shading or add three words to the stem: "(0,0) is already marked."

edits.quote: Grids drawn side by side at roughly 0.3 in (a) and 0.26 in (b) per cell, with the bottom half of the page empty
edits.fix: Children mark these squares directly, so stack the two grids or enlarge each to about 0.45 in cells using the empty half page, and leave a few lines for the pattern description.

grades-4-5.summary: Mathematically rich and well sequenced: {1,2} and {1,2,3} tables, full strategies at 100, the {1,3,4} period-7 pattern to 30 with a request to prove periodicity, contrasting rules ({1,3,5} parity, {1,4}, {1,4,5} period 8), the effect of adding a third move, inverse problems including an impossible case, and two-pile grids that lead toward Sprague-Grundy values. All answers check out. The edits are the P7(d) finite-rule ambiguity, a weak example set in P6, small P8 grids, and the footer.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 band develops the {1,3,4} game from classification to testing claims (including the wrong greedy move) to extrapolation and two-row sums, with correct answers and almost no excess text.
overall.weakest: The 4-5 page has the only real mathematical snag: P7(d) is ambiguous about whether a rule may be an infinite list, and P6 gives only one changing example to generalize from. K-1 is the band most likely to run slightly short for a quick child.
